ceb.title: How the Church Interprets Scripture
ceb.question: Why can't every believer just read the Bible and interpret it for themselves under the Holy Spirit?
ceb.answer: Scripture itself warns against purely private interpretation: St. Peter says no prophecy of Scripture is a matter of personal interpretation (2 Pet 1:20), and that the unlearned distort Paul's letters to their own destruction (2 Pet 3:16). When the Ethiopian eunuch was reading Isaiah, Philip asked if he understood, and he replied, 'How can I, unless someone guides me?' (Acts 8:31). The Church interprets Scripture according to its literal, allegorical, moral, and anagogical senses, in harmony with the whole of Tradition and the analogy of faith. The multiplication of contradictory interpretations that followed the principle of private judgment demonstrates its instability. Catholics still read and pray Scripture personally, but final judgment on its authentic meaning belongs to the living Magisterium guided by the Holy Spirit, not to each isolated reader.

en.answer_full:
> "The Church is the pillar and ground of the truth. What, then, is the pillar? The Church of the living God."
> — St. John Chrysostom, *Homilies on 1 Timothy*, Homily 11 (c. 398 AD)

The question of how Scripture is to be interpreted is not peripheral — it is the hinge on which Reformation-era Christianity pivots. The Protestant principle of **sola scriptura** — Scripture alone as the supreme rule of faith — combined with the assertion that every believer can interpret Scripture under the Spirit's guidance, has produced one of the most fragmented religious landscapes in history: over 40,000 Christian denominations, each claiming biblical authority for contradictory positions. The Catholic position, by contrast, holds that Scripture must be read within the living Tradition of the Church, interpreted by the Magisterium that Christ himself established and the Spirit guides.

---

## The Biblical Problem: Scripture Warns Against Private Interpretation

### 2 Peter 3:16 — Hard to Understand

*"In them there are some things hard to understand that the ignorant and unstable distort to their own destruction, just as they do the other scriptures"* (2 Peter 3:16, NABRE). Peter explicitly states that Paul's letters are susceptible to distortion by untrained readers. He does not say "read them carefully and the Spirit will guide you" — he warns that misreading leads to *destruction*. This presupposes that an authoritative standard of interpretation exists beyond the individual reader.

### 2 Peter 1:20 — No Private Interpretation

*"Know this first of all, that there is no prophecy of scripture that is a matter of personal interpretation"* (2 Peter 1:20, NABRE). The Greek *idias epilyseos* ("one's own interpretation") is a direct prohibition on making one's own private judgment the interpretive norm for prophetic Scripture. Peter presents Scripture as a communal possession, interpreted within the community of faith.

### Acts 8:30–31 — The Ethiopian Eunuch

When Philip encounters the Ethiopian reading Isaiah, he asks: *"Do you understand what you are reading?"* The eunuch replies: *"How can I, unless someone instructs me?"* (Acts 8:30–31, NABRE). This exchange is the New Testament's paradigm for Bible reading: the text requires a teacher. Philip, acting as the Church's representative, expounds the Scripture's meaning. Individual reading without instruction is portrayed as insufficient.

---

## Positive Biblical Evidence

### Luke 10:16 — The Authority of the Apostolic Teach

*"Whoever listens to you listens to me. Whoever rejects you rejects me"* (Luke 10:16, NABRE). Jesus identifies his own authority with that of the apostles he sends. Rejecting their teaching is rejecting him. This binding authority was transmitted through apostolic succession to the bishops of the Church.

### John 16:13 — The Spirit Guides the Church

*"When he comes, the Spirit of truth, he will guide you to all truth"* (John 16:13, NABRE). The promise of the Spirit's guidance is made to the apostolic community — "you" is plural, addressed to the Twelve. It is not a promise to every future individual reader but to the Church as a body.

### Matthew 18:17 — The Church as Final Arbiter

*"If he refuses to listen to them, tell the church. If he refuses to listen even to the church, then treat him as you would a Gentile"* (Matthew 18:17, NABRE). Jesus explicitly designates the Church — not Scripture, not the individual — as the final authority in resolving disputes among believers.

---

## The Core Theological Distinction: Magisterium vs. Private Judgment

| Authority | Nature | Guarantee |
|-----------|--------|-----------|
| **Private interpretation** | Individual reading under subjective Spirit-guidance | No external check; produces endless fragmentation |
| **Magisterium** | Apostolically-grounded authoritative teaching office | Protected from formal error by the Spirit's guidance; in continuity with apostolic tradition |

The Magisterium does not create new doctrine — it authentically *interprets* the fixed deposit of faith closed at the death of the last apostle. The Church is not above Scripture; she serves it as its guardian and interpreter.

---

## Church Fathers

> "Scripture is not in the reading but in the understanding."
> — St. Jerome, *Letter 119* (c. 406 AD)

Jerome, the greatest biblical scholar of the ancient Church, understood that right understanding requires formation — not merely literacy.

> "Wherever you see those possessed of the gifts of the Spirit claiming authority from the Scriptures — beware. The devil himself quotes Scripture."
> — St. John Chrysostom, *Homilies on Matthew*, Homily 5 (c. 390 AD)

Chrysostom recognizes that the appeal to Scripture alone cannot distinguish orthodoxy from heresy — heretics have always used Scripture to support their errors.

> "We have learned the plan of our salvation from no other than those through whom the Gospel has come down to us, which they first preached, and then, by the will of God, transmitted in writing to be the foundation and pillar of our faith."
> — St. Irenaeus of Lyon, *Against Heresies*, III.1.1 (c. 180 AD)

Irenaeus insists that the Gospel comes to us through the apostles and their successors — the written text is inseparable from the living tradition that transmits and interprets it.

---

## Ecumenical Council: Vatican I (1870)

The First Vatican Council defined the scope of authentic interpretation:

> *"It is not permissible for anyone to interpret Holy Scripture in a sense contrary to this, or indeed against the unanimous consent of the Fathers."*

The Council locates the norm of interpretation in the patristic consensus and the Magisterium — not in the individual reader.

---

## CCC References

| Reference | Teaching |
|-----------|----------|
| CCC 85 | The task of authentically interpreting the Word of God has been entrusted solely to the Magisterium |
| CCC 119 | It is the task of exegetes to work toward a better understanding and explanation of the meaning of Scripture |
| CCC 113 | Scripture is to be read in the same Spirit in which it was written — within the living Tradition of the Church |
| CCC 111 | The interpreter must be attentive to the literary forms, historical context, and unity of Scripture |

---

## Common Objections

**"The Holy Spirit is sufficient to guide me — I don't need the Church."**

If the Spirit guides individuals infallibly to correct interpretation, why do Spirit-filled Protestants contradict each other on nearly every doctrinal question? The Spirit does not give contradictory guidance. The very fragmentation of Protestantism is evidence that subjective Spirit-appeal cannot replace an objective teaching authority.

**"Catholics are just told what to think — they can't read for themselves."**

The Church has always encouraged Scripture reading. The Catechism calls Scripture "the soul of theology." What Catholics reject is not Bible reading but the claim that private interpretation is *sufficient* — the claim 2 Peter itself rejects. Catholics read Scripture within the framework of apostolic Tradition, which enriches rather than replaces personal reading.

**"The Fathers interpreted Scripture differently from each other too."**

The Fathers disagreed on secondary matters — but on the core doctrines of Trinity, Incarnation, Baptism, and Eucharist, they spoke with overwhelming consensus. It is precisely this patristic consensus that the Magisterium synthesizes and transmits. Individual patristic disagreements are far less significant than the massive disagreement produced by five centuries of the "every reader is their own interpreter" principle.

---

Scripture and the Church cannot be separated. The Bible is the Church's book — she received it from the apostles, defined its canon, copied it through the centuries, and continues to interpret it through the Magisterium that Christ established. To read Scripture faithfully is to read it within this living tradition — not as a solitary interpreter, but as a member of the body of Christ that has been promised the Spirit's guidance from the beginning.
